abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Manuka honey is widely recognized for its wound-healing properties; however, its clinical use is limited by high cost, restricted availability, and increasing concerns regarding adulteration. This study provides a preliminary comparative evaluation of Egyptian fennel (Foeniculum vulgare) honey and certified Manuka honey to investigate the potential of fennel honey as a natural product for wound-healing applications. The botanical origin of fennel honey was confirmed by melissopalynological analysis. Physicochemical properties, total phenolic and flavonoid contents, and qualitative phytochemical composition were characterized by LC-MS. Biological activity was assessed through cytocompatibility, antibacterial activity against Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and scratch wound-healing assays using Vero and human skin fibroblast cells. Potential molecular mechanisms were explored using network pharmacology and molecular docking. Fennel honey exhibited lower moisture content and slightly higher total flavonoid content than Manuka honey. Qualitative LC-MS profiling revealed both shared and distinctive metabolites, with rosmarinic acid identified as a characteristic constituent of fennel honey, while methylglyoxal was qualitatively detected in both samples. Both honeys showed comparable cytocompatibility and species-dependent antibacterial activity. In the scratch assay, fennel honey promoted greater wound closure than Manuka honey at 100 µg mL−1 after 48 h (66.0% vs. 50.4%). Network pharmacology predicted the PI3K–Akt signaling pathway as a potential target, while molecular docking suggested favorable binding of quercitrin to PI3K (−10.1 kcal mol−1). These preliminary findings identify Egyptian fennel honey as a promising natural product for further wound-healing research. However, the qualitative phytochemical analysis, in vitro biological evaluation, and computational predictions require validation by quantitative chemical profiling, mechanistic studies, and in vivo investigations before definitive conclusions can be drawn.
Qualitative LC-MS profiling, in vitro evaluation, and in silico analyses reveal promising wound-related bioactivity of Egyptian fennel honey.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Honey has been used therapeutically since antiquity, with the Egyptian Smith Papyrus (circa 2600–2200 BC) prescribing honey-based salves for open wounds, and similar formulations appearing in ancient Assyrian, Chinese, Greek, and Roman texts.1 Its high osmolarity, acidity, and enzymatic hydrogen peroxide generation were empirically harnessed to prevent infection and promote tissue repair. Although antibiotics initially relegated honey to folk medicine, the crisis of antimicrobial resistance has catalyzed renewed scientific interest, with contemporary research validating honey's multifaceted mechanisms, from osmotic dehydration of bacteria to modulation of host inflammatory pathways, and positioning it as a complementary wound management strategy.2

Among therapeutic honeys, Manuka honey (from Leptospermum scoparium nectar) has emerged as the clinical gold standard due to its non-peroxide antibacterial activity (NPA). Unlike conventional honeys that rely predominantly on glucose oxidase-derived hydrogen peroxide, Manuka's potent bactericidal action persists when peroxide is neutralized, attributable to methylglyoxal (MGO) a dicarbonyl compound formed by non-enzymatic conversion of nectar-derived dihydroxyacetone (DHA).3 Genuine Manuka samples contain up to 800 mg kg−1 MGO, correlating linearly with antibacterial potency, and efficacy against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and vancomycin-resistant Enterococci (VRE) has been demonstrated in clinical trials.4 Regulatory approval (e.g., U.S. FDA) and commercial products such as MediHoney® capitalize on its ability to debride necrotic tissue, disrupt biofilms, and accelerate re-epithelialization.5,6

However, Manuka honey's broader adoption is constrained by economic, logistical, and regulatory challenges. Geographical exclusivity limited to the four-to-six-week flowering season of L. scoparium in New Zealand and parts of Australia coupled with lengthy post-harvest maturation, drives prohibitive production costs.7 High demand and limited supply have incentivized adulteration practices, including sugar syrup dilution.8 While rigorous quality controls such as Unique Manuka Factor (UMF™) certification and spectroscopic authentication add further expense and complexity.9 This cycle of scarcity, cost, and fraud highlights the need for alternative apitherapeutics with comparable clinical benefits and fewer systemic vulnerabilities.

Fennel honey produced by bees foraging on Foeniculum vulgare presents a compelling candidate. Fennel is a hardy perennial cultivated and naturalized throughout the Mediterranean and temperate regions worldwide, ensuring broader availability and reduced dependence on narrow flowering windows.10 Phytochemical analyses reveal a rich profile of phenolic acids (gallic, caffeic, and ferulic acids) and flavonoids (quercetin, kaempferol) conferring significant antioxidant and antimicrobial activities, while volatile constituents such as trans-anethole and estragole demonstrate intrinsic anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial effects.11 This suggests fennel honey's therapeutic potential derives from synergistic phytochemical combinations rather than a single dominant compound.

Recent in vitro studies confirm fennel honey exhibits appreciable antibacterial and anti-biofilm activity against clinically relevant pathogens, with minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) against Escherichia coli, MRSA, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa within therapeutically relevant ranges and biofilm inhibition rates of approximately 60–70%.12 Fennel honey also enhances endogenous antioxidant enzymes such as glutathione peroxidase and superoxide dismutase, with its flavonoid content correlating strongly with free radical scavenging capacity critical for preventing ROS-mediated tissue damage and supporting healing. However, the existing literature remains scattered and largely descriptive, lacking direct comparisons with Manuka honey.13

Accordingly, the present study provides a comprehensive comparative evaluation of locally sourced Egyptian fennel honey and commercially certified Manuka honey by examining their physicochemical characteristics, phytochemical composition, antioxidant capacity, antimicrobial activity, and wound-healing potential. The antibacterial evaluation focused on Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa because these species are among the most prevalent bacterial pathogens isolated from acute, surgical, and chronic wound infections. Together, they represent both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria and include major biofilm-forming organisms, making them clinically relevant models for assessing the wound-healing and antimicrobial efficacy of honey-based therapies.14,15

sec.title: Melissopalynological analysis
sec.p: Melissopalynological analysis is the definitive method for confirming the botanical and geographical origin of honey based on its pollen composition. The pollen analysis in this study successfully verified the floral source of both honey samples, which is the primary step in their characterization.

The Egyptian fennel honey was classified as a unifloral honey, as pollen from Foeniculum vulgare was predominant, constituting 50% of the total pollen grains counted (Table 1, Fig. 1A). This aligns with established criteria where a pollen frequency of over 45% is required for a honey to be designated as unifloral.16 The analysis also revealed the presence of important secondary pollens, including Pimpinella anisum (anise, 20%) and Cuminum cyminum (cumin, 15%), which are characteristic of the flora in the agricultural landscapes of the Nile Delta, thereby confirming the honey's geographical origin.

Microscopic images of predominant pollen grains (400× magnification). (A) Ellipsoidal, tricolpate pollen grain of Foeniculum vulgare from fennel honey. (B) Triangular, tricolporate pollen grain of Leptospermum scoparium from Manuka honey.

sec.p: Similarly, the New Zealand Manuka honey was authenticated as a unifloral honey, with its predominant pollen identified as Leptospermum scoparium at a frequency of 60% (Table 1, Fig. 1B). This finding is strongly supported by recent research, which reported that the percentage of L. scoparium pollen in commercial Manuka honeys can range widely from 45% to 90%. The presence of Kunzea spp. (30%) as a major secondary pollen is also characteristic of New Zealand flora often found in association with L. scoparium. This pollen profile confirms the authenticity of the Manuka honey sample. Therefore, microscopic analysis serves as an indispensable tool for validating the floral identity claimed on high-value commercial honeys and for characterizing the unique attributes of regional honeys.17,18

sec.title: Water content (moisture)
sec.p: Following the botanical identification, the physicochemical properties were assessed, starting with water content, a critical parameter that influences the honey's viscosity, stability, and resistance to microbial spoilage. In this study, the moisture content of the Egyptian fennel honey was determined to be 19.0 ± 0.65%, %, while the New Zealand Manuka honey sample exhibited a higher value of 22.0 ± 0.85% (Table 1).

The 19.0% water content for the fennel honey is consistent with values reported for other fennel honeys from Egypt. For instance, studies on fennel honey from different Egyptian governorates reported moisture values ranging from 17.0% to 19.5%.19 This value falls within the internationally accepted limit (≤20%) set by the Codex Alimentarius Commission, indicating that the honey was likely harvested at an appropriate stage of maturity and possesses a low susceptibility to fermentation, which is favorable for a long shelf-life.20

Conversely, the 22.0% moisture content determined for the Manuka honey sample exceeds the maximum limit recommended by the Codex Alimentarius. While some studies on Chinese honeys have reported values over 20% due to specific production mode, this result is notably higher than the typical range of 16.0% to 19.3% previously reported for commercial Manuka honeys.21 An elevated water content above 20% significantly increases the risk of fermentation by osmophilic yeasts, which can compromise the quality and stability of the honey during storage. This high value may be attributed to several factors, including harvesting during a period of high ambient humidity, premature extraction before the bees could dehydrate the nectar to its final, stable composition, or post-harvest processing and storage conditions. This finding underscores the importance of stringent quality control for commercial honey products.

sec.title: Ash content
sec.p: The ash content of honey is an indicator of its mineral richness and is a widely recognized quality parameter. The analysis revealed that the fennel honey possessed a total ash value of 0.46% ± 0.03, while the Manuka honey had a value of 0.34% ± 0.02 (Table 2). These results suggest that the Egyptian fennel honey has a higher mineral content than the Manuka honey sample tested.

caption.title: Physicochemical characteristics and antioxidant-related properties of Egyptian fennel honey and certified Manuka honey (mean ± SD, n = 3)

sec.p: Crucially, both of these values fall well within the maximum limit of 0.6% stipulated for blossom honeys by the Codex Alimentarius Commission,22,23 confirming the good quality and authenticity of the samples. The ash content reflects the concentration of minerals absorbed by the plant from the soil, which is then transferred to the nectar. The value of 0.34% for Manuka honey is consistent with previous studies, as Manuka is known to have a higher mineral content than many lighter honeys, with typical values ranging from 0.1% to 0.3%.24,25

The higher value of 0.46% in the Egyptian fennel honey is a notable characteristic. While still compliant with international standards, it is on the higher end of the typical range for blossom honeys, suggesting a particularly rich mineral profile for this regional honey. This finding aligns with studies on other Egyptian honeys, which have demonstrated that mineral content can vary significantly based on the specific floral source and the local soil composition.26 Therefore, the analysis of ash content not only verifies the quality of both honeys but also highlights a key feature of the tested fennel honey as a potentially significant source of dietary minerals.

sec.title: Reducing sugar content
sec.p: Reducing sugars, mainly fructose and glucose, represent the largest proportion of honey's solid content. In this study, the reducing sugar content was found to be 68.9% ± 1.4 for fennel honey and 66.0% ± 2.4 for Manuka honey (Table 2). These values are consistent with the Codex Alimentarius Commission standard, which requires that authentic honey contains no less than 60% reducing sugars. Reported literature indicates that the reducing sugar content typically ranges between 60.8–76.2% for Manuka honey and 65.5–82.0% for fennel honey.19,27

sec.title: Color intensity
sec.p: The color of honey is a key characteristic that is often linked to its floral origin, mineral content, and bioactive potential. In this study, a clear difference in color intensity was observed between the two samples. Manuka honey exhibited a higher color intensity (219 ± 2 mAU) compared to fennel honey (163 ± 0.5 mAU) (Table 2), indicating a darker amber color for the Manuka sample. This finding is consistent with the general characterization of Manuka honey as typically dark honey. Honey color is influenced by pigments such as carotenoids and flavonoids derived from the botanical source, as well as the Maillard reaction during maturation and storage.28 As will be discussed, there is often a strong positive correlation between the color intensity of honey, its phenolic content, and its antioxidant activity.

sec.title: pH, free acid value, electrical conductivity and HMF content
sec.p: Both honey samples were characterized for key physicochemical parameters to facilitate comparative evaluation. Fennel honey exhibited a pH of 4.2 ± 0.08, while Manuka honey showed a slightly lower pH of 3.9 ± 0.19, consistent with values previously reported for floral honeys. Free acidity was higher in fennel honey (24.8 ± 1.3 meq kg−1) than in Manuka honey (16.0 ± 1.5 meq kg−1), suggesting a greater contribution of naturally occurring organic acids. Electrical conductivity was lower in fennel honey (0.32 ± 0.03 mS cm−1) than in Manuka honey (0.57 ± 0.05 mS cm−1), reflecting differences in mineral composition associated with their distinct botanical origins. The hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) content was 15.5 ± 2.1 mg kg−1 for fennel honey and 10.5 ± 1.8 mg kg−1 for Manuka honey. Both values were well below the accepted regulatory limits, indicating good sample quality with minimal thermal or storage-related deterioration.3,29

sec.title: Phytochemical composition and antioxidant activity
sec.p: Phenolic compounds and flavonoids are the primary phytochemicals that drive the antioxidant and other biological activities of honey. In our analysis, Manuka and fennel honey exhibited nearly identical total phenolic content (TPC) 50 ± 1.6 mg GAE per 100 g and 52 ± 1.8 mg GAE per 100 g, respectively (Table 2)findings that align well with existing literature. Fennel honey also demonstrated a slightly higher total flavonoid content (TFC) at 10.5 mg ± 0.66 QE per 100 g, compared to 8 mg ± 0.35 QE per 100 g in Manuka honey. The DPPH free radical scavenging assay further highlighted the antioxidant profiles of the two honeys. The radical inhibition (%) values closely mirrored their phenolic levels and color intensity: Manuka honey showed slightly stronger activity at 39.07 ± 1.23%, while fennel honey registered 35.96 ± 2.4% (Table 2). This similar phenolic and flavonoid profile may support the potential for comparable nutritional and therapeutic properties of both honey types.25,30

sec.title: Qualitative phytochemical profiling of manuka vs. fennel honey
sec.p: A range of phenolic acids, esters, and flavonoids were identified in both Manuka and Fennel honey samples by LC-MS. Key compounds included flavonoid glycosides (e.g., apigenin-7-O-glucoside, quercitrin), flavonols (galangin, quercetin, rhamnetin, isorhamnetin, morin), flavanones (naringenin, pinocembrin, sakuranetin), and various phenolic acids and their esters. For each compound, the molecular formula and exact mass were confirmed by the observed molecular ion peak. For instance, apigenin-7-O-glucoside (C21H20O10, exact mass 432.11 Da) was detected at a retention time (RT) of 1.67 min with a corresponding m/z of 431.2 in negative ion mode ([M − H]−). Similarly, leptosperin (C22H32O15, exact mass 536.17 Da) was observed at RT 8.6 min with an m/z of 535.2 ([M + H]+). All observed m/z values were consistent with their calculated molecular weights, confirming the identities of the compounds listed in the analysis.

The flavonoid profiles showed notable distinctions between the two honeys. Manuka honey was uniquely characterized by the presence of apigenin-7-O-glucoside (RT 1.67, [M − H]− 431.2), galangin (RT 4.07, [M − H]− 269.1), sakuranetin (RT 13.94, [M + H]+ 285.1), and rhamnetin (RT 11.07, [M − H]− 315.2). Conversely, isorhamnetin (RT 5.18, [M − H]− 315.2) and morin (RT 21.01, [M − H]− 301.02) were detected only in the Fennel sample. A significant number of flavonoids were common to both samples, including apigenin, naringenin, pinocembrin, and quercetin. The identification of these compounds aligns with existing literature, which recognizes flavonoids such as apigenin, quercetin, galangin, pinocembrin, and isorhamnetin as well-known and important constituents in Manuka and fennel honey.31,32

The phenolic acid and ester profiles also revealed key differences. Caffeic acid phenethyl ether (RT 21.07) was found only in the Manuka sample, along with free ferulic and p-coumaric acids. In contrast, rosmarinic acid (RT 13.12, [M − H]− 359.2) and malic acid (RT 6.091, [M − H]− 133.0) were exclusive to Fennel honey. Several phenolic derivatives were present in both honey types, including caffeic acid benzyl ether, the cinnamyl ester of p-coumaric acid, methyl syringate, and caftaric acid. These classes of compounds including flavonols, flavones, flavanones, and derivatives of hydroxycinnamic and benzoic acids are among the most widely reported phytochemicals in mono-floral honeys and are consistent with established phenolic profiles in literature.33

Our findings are largely consistent with the known chemical profiles of Manuka and Fennel honey. Manuka (Leptospermum scoparium) honey is renowned for specific markers such as leptosperin and high levels of methyl syringate. In a key study, leptosperin was identified as a unique chemical marker for Manuka honey. Our results corroborate these findings, as leptosperin was detected exclusively in the Manuka sample. Methyl syringate was observed in both honeys, which is not unexpected as it is found in many honey types, though its presence is considered characteristic of Manuka.31

Fennel (Foeniculum vulgare) honey is reported to be rich in hydroxycinnamic acids and related compounds. Our observation of rosmarinic acid and caffeic acid derivatives in the Fennel sample aligns with detailed LC-MS/MS studies that identified them, and vanillic as components of Fennel honey.34 In our analysis, pinocembrin was indeed found in the Fennel sample, although galangin was detected in the Manuka sample.3 Furthermore, the abundance of quercetin and its glycoside quercitrin in our Fennel sample matches reports that fennel honey is high in quercetin and can contain various quercetin derivatives.30

In summary, LC-MS analysis demonstrates that both Manuka and Fennel honey share a broadly similar phytochemical profile rich in flavonoids and phenolic compounds. However, Manuka honey is uniquely characterized by the presence of leptosperin, while Fennel honey exhibits notably higher levels of hydroxycinnamic acids especially rosmarinic acid and distinct flavonoid aglycones (Fig. S1, Table 3). As these observations are based on qualitative profiling, comprehensive quantitative metabolite analysis is required to confirm differences in the abundance of these constituents and to establish their relationship with the observed biological activities.

sec.title: Detection of methylglyoxal in fennel honey
sec.p: Methylglyoxal (MGO) is a unique component of Manuka honey largely responsible for its well-documented antimicrobial activity. To date, the presence of this metabolite in fennel honey has not been reported. In this study, derivatization with O-phenylenediamine (OPD) followed by LC/MS analysis of both honey samples revealed quinoxaline derivatives at comparable retention times and identical molecular ions. Specifically, methyl quinoxaline was identified at RT = 11.3 min with [M + H]+ = 145, while the reaction of OPD with hydroxymethylfurfural produced a derivative detected at RT = 23.7 min with [M + H]+ = 325.21 These findings suggest that, in addition to their broadly similar flavonoid and phenolic profiles, both Manuka and fennel honey contain methylglyoxal (MGO), although the present qualitative LC-MS analysis does not permit comparison of its abundance between the two honey types. Quantitative determination and standardization of MGO, together with other bioactive constituents, will be essential to establish the contribution of MGO to the antimicrobial activity of fennel honey and to evaluate its potential as a quality marker for future therapeutic applications.

sec.title: Cytotoxicity assays
sec.p: To evaluate the safety profile of the honey samples and their suitability for potential therapeutic applications, their cytotoxic effects were systematically assessed against two representative normal cell lines: Vero (monkey kidney epithelial) cells and HSF (human skin fibroblast) cells. Human skin fibroblasts (HSFs) and Vero cells were selected as complementary in vitro models for biological evaluation. HSFs were used because fibroblasts are key mediators of wound repair, contributing to collagen synthesis, extracellular matrix remodeling, and wound closure, making them a relevant model for assessing wound-healing activity. Vero cells were employed as a well-established mammalian cell line for general cytocompatibility screening. Although these models provide an appropriate preliminary assessment, they do not fully represent the complexity of wound healing. Therefore, future studies should incorporate additional cell types, including macrophages, keratinocytes, and endothelial cells, as well as more physiologically relevant co-culture or three-dimensional models.

sec.title: Effect of Manuka and Fennel honey on viability
sec.p: Both honey samples exhibited low cytotoxicity toward Vero cells under the experimental conditions. The estimated IC50 values were 5.61 mg mL−1 (95% CI: 4.42–7.13 mg mL−1) for Manuka honey and 6.57 mg mL−1 (95% CI: 5.44–7.93 mg mL−1) for fennel honey (Fig. 2a and b). These IC50 values exceeded the concentrations used in the subsequent biological assays, indicating that the tested concentrations were below the estimated cytotoxic threshold for Vero cells.

caption.title: Dose–response curves illustrating the cytotoxic effects of (A) Manuka honey and (B) Fennel honey on Vero cell viability following 48 hours of treatment, as assessed using the MTT assay. (C) Comparative viability of human skin fibroblast (HSF) cells treated with various concentrations (mg ml−1) of both honey types for 48 hours. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) from three independent replicates. Statistical significance is indicated as **p < 0.0025.

sec.p: The biocompatibility of the honeys with human skin fibroblasts is a critical parameter for their potential application as wound healing agents Sulforhodamine B (SRB) assay results revealed that both fennel and Manuka honey maintained high levels of HSF cell viability across the tested concentration range (0.1–1 mg mL−1), with cell survival consistently above the 80% cytocompatibility threshold defined by ISO 10993-5 for in vitro cytotoxicity testing (Table 3, Fig. 2c). At lower concentrations of 0.1 and 0.5 mg mL−1, both honey samples exhibited minimal impact on fibroblast viability, with cell survival consistently exceeding 95%. The observed differences between the two honey types at these concentrations were negligible and did not reach statistical significance.

However, a clear divergence emerged at the highest tested concentration of 1 mg mL−1. At this concentration, fennel honey preserved a higher cell viability of 89.9%, while Manuka honey reduced viability more markedly to 82.8%. Although both honeys can be considered nontoxic across all tested concentrations since cell viability remained above the 80% threshold indicative of cytocompatibility, the significantly greater preservation of fibroblast viability in the fennel honey group suggests a comparatively superior safety profile for dermal cells at higher therapeutic doses. This finding is particularly noteworthy, as the ability to maintain fibroblast proliferation at effective concentrations is a highly desirable characteristic for wound healing agents, supporting tissue regeneration without compromising cellular function.

sec.title: Effect of Manuka and Fennel honey on wound healing of human skin fibroblasts (HSF)
sec.p: The effects of fennel and Manuka honey on wound closure were evaluated using an in vitro scratch assay in human skin fibroblasts (HSFs) at 24 and 48 h (Fig. 3 and S2). Both honey samples promoted wound closure in a time- and concentration-dependent manner. At 100 µg mL−1, fennel honey produced moderately greater wound closure than Manuka honey at both 24 h (28.7% vs. 14.1%) and 48 h (66.0% vs. 50.4%). In contrast, at 500 µg mL−1, both honeys produced comparable responses after 48 h, achieving wound closure of 78.3% and 77.9% for fennel and Manuka honey, respectively, compared with 63.2% in the untreated control.

caption.title: Percentage of wound closure in human skin fibroblasts (HSF) after treatment with different concentration of Fennel and Manuka honey over 24 and 48 h. Data are presented as mean ± SD. **p < 0.001, vs. control group.

sec.p: The moderate differences observed at the lower concentration may reflect variations in the chemical composition of the two honeys, as suggested by the qualitative LC-MS analysis, although the contribution of individual constituents cannot be determined from the present study. The comparable responses observed at the higher concentration indicate that both honeys are capable of enhancing fibroblast-mediated wound closure under the experimental conditions employed.

It should be noted that the scratch assay is a simplified two-dimensional in vitro model that primarily reflects collective cell migration together with contributions from cell proliferation and does not fully recapitulate the complexity of wound healing in vivo. Consequently, the present findings should be regarded as preliminary and should not be interpreted as evidence of superior wound-healing efficacy. Further studies incorporating three-dimensional wound models, mechanistic investigations, and in vivo validation will be necessary to determine the biological significance of the observed differences.

Several naturally derived flavonoids and phenolic acids have been investigated for their capacity to promote wound healing through diverse mechanisms, including modulation of inflammation, enhancement of collagen deposition, and antioxidant activity.35 Apigenin has demonstrated pro-healing effects by accelerating keratinocyte migration and re-epithelialization in excision and diabetic wound models, primarily through anti-inflammatory action and promotion of fibroblast proliferation.36,37 Naringenin has similarly been shown to enhance wound closure and collagen maturation in full-thickness skin wounds in rats, with reported reduction of local inflammatory cytokines and oxidative stress.38,39 Pinocembrin has been reported to stimulate migration and proliferation of human keratinocytes in scratch assays, and limited in vivo evidence suggests it supports healing in burn wounds, likely through antioxidant-mediated cytoprotection.40,41

Quercetin has been extensively studied for cutaneous wound repair; topical quercetin and quercetin enriched dressings have consistently improved angiogenesis, collagen deposition, and epithelial regeneration, partly attributable to its potent free radical scavenging activity.42,43 Morin has exhibited comparable effects, enhancing granulation tissue formation, collagen synthesis, and reducing inflammatory infiltration in experimental wounds.44 Caffeic acid, predominantly investigated in murine excision wound models, has been shown to promote fibroblast proliferation, increase hydroxyproline content, and accelerate wound contraction.45

Rosmarinic acid has demonstrated wound healing potential both in vitro and in vivo, with evidence of faster scratch closure in keratinocyte assays and improved collagen organization and reduced inflammation in animal models.46 In contrast, direct evidence for methyl syringate, isorhamnetin, and quercitrin remains limited. While these compounds possess recognized antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, their specific effects on wound healing have not been systematically characterized in animal models or cell-based assays, and available data are largely extrapolated from studies of related glycosides or parent aglycones.47–49

Overall, these data highlight the potential of fennel honey as a more effective promoter of wound closure at lower concentrations, while both fennel and manuka honey demonstrate robust wound healing activity at higher concentrations.

This suggests that fennel honey may offer advantages where lower doses are desirable, potentially reducing cost and minimizing any concentration related cytotoxic effects. Further mechanistic studies would be valuable to elucidate the specific pathways through which fennel honey enhances wound healing and to explore its clinical relevance as a complementary or alternative therapeutic agent to manuka honey.

sec.title: Antimicrobial activity
sec.p: The antibacterial activity of Manuka and Egyptian fennel honey was evaluated by determining the minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) against Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 29213, Escherichia coli ATCC 25922, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa ATCC 27853 (Table 2). Manuka honey exhibited greater activity against S. aureus, with an MIC of 100 ± 5.0 mg mL−1 compared with 115 ± 7.0 mg mL−1 for fennel honey. Conversely, fennel honey showed lower MIC values against E. coli (110 ± 5.0 vs. 150 ± 7.6 mg mL−1) and P. aeruginosa (220 ± 8.6 vs. 250 ± 12.2 mg mL−1), indicating enhanced activity against the tested Gram-negative strains. Despite these differences, P. aeruginosa was the least susceptible organism for both honey samples, consistent with its intrinsic resistance to antimicrobial agents (Table 4).

sec.p: The species dependent antibacterial activity observed in this study agrees with previous reports demonstrating that the antimicrobial efficacy of honey is strongly influenced by its botanical origin and chemical composition. The superior activity of Manuka honey against S. aureus is consistent with its well-established non peroxide antibacterial activity, largely attributed to methylglyoxal and other bioactive constituents. In contrast, the comparatively greater activity of fennel honey against the Gram-negative strains suggests that its antimicrobial profile is governed by a different combination of phytochemicals. Qualitative LC-MS analysis identified several phenolic acids and flavonoids that may contribute to this activity; however, the present data do not permit attribution of the antibacterial effect to specific metabolites.

Nevertheless, these conclusions should be regarded as preliminary because the phytochemical characterization was qualitative and the antimicrobial evaluation was limited to three reference strains. Quantitative determination of key antibacterial constituents, including methylglyoxal and major phenolic compounds, together with minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC), time-kill, and mechanistic studies using clinical multidrug-resistant isolates, will be required to establish the chemical basis of the observed antibacterial activity.

sec.title: Network pharmacology analysis
sec.p: Network pharmacology was employed as a hypothesis generating approach to explore the potential molecular mechanisms underlying the wound-healing activity of fennel honey. Target prediction identified 181 putative targets associated with fennel honey, while 2763 wound healing related targets were retrieved from disease databases. Comparison of these datasets identified 252 overlapping targets, which were subjected to Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses (Fig. 4).

caption.title: GO and KEGG pathway enrichment analysis for fennel honey targets. (A–C) Bar plots of the top enriched Gene Ontology terms for biological processes (A), molecular functions (B), and cellular components (C). Bar length corresponds to gene count, and color indicates the adjusted p-value. (D) Bubble chart of the top enriched KEGG pathways (KEGG permission ref. 254261) Bubble size reflects gene count, the x-axis represents the gene ratio, and color indicates the adjusted p-value.

sec.p: GO biological process analysis revealed significant enrichment of targets involved in cellular responses to chemical and oxidative stress, regulation of inflammatory responses, cytokine production, apoptosis, and responses to bacterial derived molecules (Fig. 4a). These processes are closely associated with the regulation of the wound microenvironment, where coordinated control of inflammation, oxidative stress, and cell survival is essential for efficient tissue repair. Cellular component analysis showed enrichment in membrane rafts, membrane microdomains, focal adhesions, caveolae, and vesicular compartments (Fig. 4b), suggesting that many predicted targets are localized to signaling complexes involved in cell adhesion, migration, and intercellular communication. Molecular function analysis further identified enrichment of cytokine receptor binding, cytokine activity, growth factor receptor binding, and transcription factor binding (Fig. 4c), supporting the potential involvement of fennel honey constituents in pathways regulating inflammatory signaling and tissue regeneration.

KEGG pathway analysis identified the PI3K–Akt signaling pathway as the most significantly enriched pathway (Fig. 4d), followed by the AGE–RAGE signaling pathway and several inflammation and infection related pathways. The PI3K–Akt pathway is a well-established regulator of cell survival, proliferation, migration, angiogenesis, and extracellular matrix remodeling, all of which contribute to wound repair. Network analysis further highlighted PIK3CA, PIK3R1, AKT1, MAPK1, and MAPK3 as the principal hub genes, reflecting their extensive involvement across the enriched pathways and suggesting that they may represent key nodes within the predicted wound healing network.

Collectively, these analyses provide a plausible mechanistic framework linking the phytochemical constituents of fennel honey to biological pathways involved in tissue repair. However, it is important to emphasize that network pharmacology is a computational, hypothesis generating approach based on predicted target interactions and pathway enrichment. Consequently, the identified pathways and hub genes should not be interpreted as experimentally validated mechanisms but rather as candidates for future investigation. Validation using molecular techniques, such as gene or protein expression analysis and pathway activation studies, will be required to confirm the involvement of PI3K–Akt signaling and other predicted pathways in the wound-healing activity of fennel honey.

Interestingly, previous studies have shown that KRAS, RAF1, MAPK1, and MAPK3 coordinate keratinocyte proliferation and migration processes are essential for rapid re-epithelialization.50–52 KRAS acts as a critical upstream molecular switch, relaying growth factor signals into the MAPK cascade and triggering cell cycle entry and directed migration. RAF1 further influences cytoskeletal remodeling through regulation of Rho GTPases, while downstream MAPK1 and MAPK3 (ERK2 and ERK1) activate transcriptional programs that stimulate keratinocyte proliferation at the wound edge.53

In parallel, the PI3K/AKT axis comprising PIK3CA, PIK3R1, and AKT1promotes cell survival and supports angiogenesis, both of which are critical for new tissue formation. Activation of PIK3CA leads to PIP3 accumulation, recruiting AKT1 to stimulate endothelial proliferation and vascular stabilization, thus enhancing nutrient delivery to regenerating tissue.54–56 PIK3R1 provides regulatory feedback to restrain excessive activation; its loss has been linked to increased fibroblast migration and collagen deposition.57

The NF-κB pathway, through RELA and NFKB1, integrates inflammatory and survival signals throughout wound healing. Its early activation in immune and epithelial cells promotes cytokine expression and leukocyte recruitment, facilitating initial wound debridement. Importantly, NF-κB remains active in myofibroblasts during the remodeling phase, where it prevents apoptosis and supports extracellular matrix turnover. However, prolonged activation may predispose to pathological fibrosis, underscoring the importance of temporal regulation.58,59

Taken together, these studies suggest that the top KEGG-enriched targets identified for fennel honey metabolites converge on core regulators of wound healing, spanning proliferation, migration, angiogenesis, and matrix remodeling. This mechanistic alignment provides a plausible molecular explanation for the experimentally observed wound healing activity of fennel honey and supports further pharmacological investigation.

Notably, the observed effect of fennel honey was modest at 24 h but became more pronounced at 48 h. This likely reflects the time dependent activation of these pathways: during the early repair phase (∼24 h), the response is dominated by inflammation and immune recruitment primarily driven by NF-κB, whereas the proliferative phase (∼48 h) requires robust proliferation and migration regulated by KRAS, RAF1, MAPK1/3.

It is therefore reasonable to hypothesize that the predicted interactions between fennel honey constituents and KEGG-enriched targets may be consistent with biological processes associated with the 48 h stage of wound healing, including epithelial expansion, angiogenesis, and early tissue remodeling. These computational predictions provide a plausible mechanistic framework that may explain the enhanced wound closure observed experimentally at this time point; however, they should be regarded as hypothesis generating and require validation through appropriate molecular and functional studies.

sec.title: Molecular docking
sec.p: Since PI3K emerged as the most significantly enriched target associated with the wound healing activity of fennel honey constituents, molecular docking analysis was undertaken to identify the bioactive compounds most likely to contribute to this effect. A cavity search conducted using the CB-Dock2 server identified five putative binding pockets within the PI3K structure, each implicated in regulating the enzyme's function. Notably, Sites 1 and 5 are positioned at the interface between the catalytic p110 subunit and the regulatory p85 subunit, where they modulate critical protein–protein interactions; disruption of these interactions is known to facilitate PI3K activation. In contrast, Site 2 encompasses the ATP binding catalytic site, which directly mediates the enzyme's kinase activity and triggers activation of downstream signaling pathways. Additionally, Sites 3 and 4 represent predicted allosteric pockets suggested to stabilize the enzyme's catalytic conformation without altering its basal state.60

Hence, we investigated the ability of different components of fennel honey to bind to the different aforementioned sites. The molecular docking analysis showed that compounds based on a flavonoid scaffold consistently outperform the other phenolic structures. The top seven compounds in terms of average and best scores,Quercitrin, Isorhamnetin, Quercetin, Naringenin, Apigenin, Rosmarinic acid, and Morin, share this core structural motif or similar poly-phenolic features. This suggests that the rigid, planar ring system and the specific arrangement of hydroxyl groups characteristic of flavonoids provide a privileged framework for interacting with multiple pockets on the PI3K surface. Conversely, two compounds, Methyl Syringate and Pinocembrin, demonstrate consistently poor performance. With binding energies weaker than −6.0 kcal mol−1 across nearly all sites, their scores are indicative of weak and likely nonspecific interaction.

At Site 1, located at the p110/p85 protein–protein interaction (PPI) interface, Quercitrin emerged as the most promising ligand, exhibiting an exceptionally strong binding energy of −10.1 kcal mol−1. This value is notably high for a small molecule targeting a challenging PPI surface, suggesting the formation of a highly stable and specific complex. Other flavonoids, including Isorhamnetin (−8.7 kcal mol−1), Quercetin (−8.5 kcal mol−1), and Morin (−8.1 kcal mol−1), also demonstrated substantial affinity, collectively underscoring the suitability of the flavonoid scaffold for modulating PI3K activation via interface disruption.

On the other hand, Site 2, the ATP catalytic site responsible for the enzyme's kinase activity, Quercitrin again ranked as the top binder (−9.1 kcal mol−1). This potent affinity supports its potential as a competitive orthosteric inhibitor. Rosmarinic acid and Isorhamnetin (both −8.5 kcal mol−1), along with Quercetin (−8.4 kcal mol−1), also showed significant binding, suggesting their candidacy for directly modulating catalytic function.

At the allosteric pockets, distinct trends were observed. Site 3, predicted to stabilize the enzyme's catalytic conformation, showed highest affinity for Quercetin (−8.1 kcal mol−1), closely followed by Naringenin (−8.1 kcal mol−1), Isorhamnetin (−8.0 kcal mol−1), and Rosmarinic acid (−8.0 kcal mol−1). These results identify them as promising scaffolds for non-competitive, allosteric modulation. Conversely, Site 4 appeared less accommodating overall; Quercitrin and Rosmarinic acid achieved modest binding energies (−7.9 kcal mol−1), with Quercetin and Isorhamnetin slightly lower (−7.8 kcal mol−1). While weaker than Site 3, these values still suggest possible avenues for designing selective allosteric inhibitors.

Finally, Site 5, a secondary p110/p85 interface site, Quercitrin again led (−8.3 kcal mol−1), followed by Isorhamnetin and Morin (both −8.1 kcal mol−1). These findings reinforce the idea that the flavonoid core structure effectively engages multiple surfaces critical for PI3K regulation.

A comparative structure–activity relationship (SAR) analysis further revealed that the addition of a rhamnose moiety to Quercetin to yield Quercitrin substantially enhanced binding affinity at the interface site (site 1, –10.1 kcal mol−1, an improvement of −1.6 kcal mol−1) and the ATP site (site 2, –9.1 kcal mol−1, improvement of −0.7 kcal mol−1). In contrast, this glycosylation had negligible or slightly adverse effects on the allosteric sites. Fig. 5. Summarize binding energy of compounds with different pockets of PI3K.

The heatmap displays the calculated binding energies (kcal mol−1) for ten selected compounds at five different binding sites of the target protein. sec.p: Hence, Quercitrin showed remarkable binding affinity to different pockets of PI3K (Fig. 6), it was selected for studying its interaction with the amino acid residues. At site 1, Quercitrin engages multiple polar and charged residues critical for maintaining the structural integrity of the interface. Key hydrogen bonds are formed with ARG662, ARG818, and ASP626, which help anchor the ligand within the pocket and stabilize its orientation. A pi-cation interaction is observed between Quercitrin's aromatic system and LYS271, adding further electrostatic stabilization. Additionally, residues such as MET811, PRO835, and GLU849 contribute to the complex through additional hydrogen bonds or hydrophobic contacts, supporting an extensive and cooperative binding network. Quercitrin engages several key residues through hydrogen bonding, notably with ASN377 and ASN378, which help anchor the ligand in the nucleotide binding pocket. Additional hydrogen bonds are observed with GLY364 and HIS362, which are proximal to the catalytic core and contribute to correct positioning of the ligand relative to the ATP site.

caption.title: Molecular docking poses of quercitrin within the PI3K binding sites. The central panel shows the crystallographic structure of PI3Kα (PDB: 3HHM) in a ribbon diagram, with quercitrin (CPK model) docked into five distinct sites (S1–S5). The surrounding panels provide 2D representations of the detailed molecular interactions between quercitrin and amino acid residues at each respective binding site (S1–S5).

sec.p: While in case of site 2, a notable pi-cation interaction is formed between Quercitrin's aromatic system and LYS548, a residue frequently implicated in coordinating the phosphate groups of ATP, suggesting that Quercitrin could competitively occupy the ATP site and hinder substrate access. Furthermore, hydrophobic and van der Waals contacts involving TRP574 and LEU570 further stabilize the ligand, with LEU570 participating in a pi-alkyl interaction that complements the polar network.

Docking of Quercitrin at Site 3, identified as a putative allosteric site on PI3K, revealed a balanced combination of polar and hydrophobic interactions that likely contribute to its moderate predicted binding affinity (−8.1 kcal mol−1). Key hydrogen bonds are formed with GLU78 and ARG79, residues positioned near the edge of the pocket, which anchor the rhamnose moiety of Quercitrin and help orient the ligand correctly within the binding cavity. Another stabilizing hydrogen bond is observed with ARG693, adding further polarity driven stabilization on the opposite side of the molecule.

Additionally, a series of hydrophobic and pi-alkyl interactions involve VAL125, ILE112, LYS111, and ARG115, which interact with the polyphenolic core of Quercitrin. These contacts likely enhance ligand accommodation within the relatively shallow and less solvent exposed environment of the allosteric pocket. The combination of these hydrophobic contacts and peripheral polar interactions suggests that Quercitrin can occupy this site without inducing large conformational changes in the enzyme's ground state, consistent with the predicted role of this pocket in modulating PI3K catalytic efficiency indirectly.

In the second allosteric pocket, site 4, quercitrin established several hydrogen bonds with residues near the pocket entrance, notably ASP337, ILE338, and SER361, which help to anchor the sugar moiety and the polyphenolic core in the correct orientation.

In addition, Quercitrin forms multiple pi-cation and electrostatic interactions involving ARG1023, ASP1029, and LYS1024, residues positioned deeper within the pocket that likely contribute to stabilizing the complex. A further pi-alkyl interaction with ARG340 complements the polar network, reflecting the hybrid character of the binding environment at this site.

While the overall binding affinity at Site 4 is slightly lower than at the ATP catalytic site or PPI interface, the presence of both hydrophilic and hydrophobic contacts supports the idea that Quercitrin may function as a non-competitive allosteric modulator, subtly influencing PI3K catalytic efficiency without directly blocking the active site.

At Site 5, corresponding to a secondary p110/p85 protein–protein interaction interface on PI3K, revealed a focused set of polar contacts contributing to its moderate binding affinity (−8.3 kcal mol−1). Key hydrogen bonds were observed with ASN677, HIS676, and SER474, stabilizing the ligand's orientation within the interface pocket. Additional hydrogen bonding with TYR556 supports further anchoring, particularly along the planar polyphenolic scaffold of Quercitrin. Complementing these polar interactions, a pi-alkyl contact was identified with LYS678, providing hydrophobic stabilization at the pocket's boundary. This pattern suggests that although Site 5 is less deeply recessed compared to the primary PPI site (Site 1), Quercitrin's hydroxyl rich structure can still effectively engage key residues and potentially perturb protein–protein interactions.

Overall, these results reinforce the adaptability of the flavonoid scaffold in modulating distinct regions of the p110/p85 interface. The combination of polar and limited hydrophobic contacts at Site 5 points toward a role for Quercitrin as a potential PPI modulator, supporting its candidacy in natural product–driven strategies to fine tune PI3K activity in wound healing contexts. Fig. 6 illustrates the different binding mode of quercitrin with PI3K.

However, these observations are derived solely from molecular docking and should be regarded as hypothesis generating rather than confirmatory. Experimental studies are therefore required to validate quercitrin binding and determine its effect on PI3K activity in the context of wound healing. Fig. 6 illustrates the predicted binding mode of quercitrin within the PI3K binding site.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study provides a preliminary comparative evaluation of Egyptian fennel honey and Manuka honey with respect to their physicochemical characteristics, phytochemical composition, antibacterial activity, and wound healing potential. Qualitative LC-MS profiling revealed both shared and distinctive metabolites, suggesting that the two honeys contain a common core of bioactive phenolic acids and flavonoids while differing in several botanical marker compounds. In vitro studies demonstrated that both honeys enhanced fibroblast wound closure and exhibited antibacterial activity, although their antimicrobial efficacy was species dependent, with Manuka honey showing greater activity against Staphylococcus aureus and fennel honey exhibiting lower MIC values against Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa under the present experimental conditions.

Network pharmacology and molecular docking further identified the PI3K–Akt signaling pathway as a potential target associated with the wound healing activity of fennel honey and predicted favorable interactions between quercitrin and PI3K. However, these computational analyses are hypothesis generating tools and should not be considered mechanistic evidence without experimental validation.

Overall, the present work identifies Egyptian fennel honey as a promising natural product for further investigation in wound healing research. Future work should include quantitative metabolomics, standardized MGO determination, mechanistic validation, animal wound models, and ultimately controlled clinical evaluation.

sec.title: Melissopalynological analysis
sec.p: Two botanically distinct honey samples were investigated in this study. Egyptian fennel (Foeniculum vulgare) honey was obtained directly from apiaries in Moabddah Village, Abanoub, Assiut Governorate, Egypt. Certified Manuka (Leptospermum scoparium) honey was purchased as a commercial product (3Bee, New Zealand) with a labeled Unique Manuka Factor (UMF) of 10+ and a methylglyoxal (MGO) rating of 263+. To verify the botanical origin of both honey samples, melissopalynological analysis was performed through qualitative microscopic examination of the pollen sediment following standard procedures.61

For the preparation of slides without acetolysis, a 10 g aliquot of each honey sample was dissolved in 20 mL of distilled water warmed to 40 °C. The solution was centrifuged at 2500 rpm for 10 minutes, and the supernatant was subsequently decanted. To ensure the complete removal of sugars, the sediment was resuspended in approximately 10 mL of distilled water and centrifuged a second time for 10 minutes. The entire final sediment was then spread onto a glass slide (20 × 20 mm). For samples identified as being poor in pollen, a larger starting quantity of 20 g of honey was used. Conversely, if a sample was exceptionally rich in sediment, the residue was distributed between two cover glasses. The prepared slides were gently dried at a temperature not exceeding 40 °C. Finally, the sediment was mounted using Kaiser's glycerin gelatin, which was liquified in a 40 °C water bath prior to application.

For microscopic examination, pollen grains were identified by comparison with reference literature and comparative slides. A complete analysis was performed by identifying and counting a total of 100 pollen grains to determine their relative frequencies. Pollen frequencies were classified as “very frequent” (>45%), “frequent” (16–45%), “rare” (3–15%), and “sporadic” (<3%). Other constituents of the sediment, such as granulated matter indicative of honeydew, were also noted.

sec.title: Water content
sec.p: The water content (%) of the honey samples was determined by measuring the refractive index using an Abbe refractometer (Shanghai Yueping Scientific Instrument Co., Ltd, Shanghai, China) at 20 °C, according to the official methods of analysis of honey.23

sec.title: Ash content
sec.p: To determine the total ash content, approximately 5 g of each honey sample was placed in a pre-weighed vitreosil basin. The sample was gently heated until charring was complete, and no more fumes were emitted. The charred material was then incinerated in a muffle furnace at a temperature of 550–600 °C for 4–5 hours. After incineration, the furnace was allowed to cool to 150 °C, and the basin was transferred to a desiccator to cool to room temperature before being weighed. The percentage of total ash was calculated as the ratio of the weight of the ash to the initial weight of the sample, multiplied by 100.

sec.title: Reducing sugar content
sec.p: The concentration of reducing sugars was quantified using the dinitro-salicylic acid (DNS; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA)method as described by,62 with minor modifications. One gram of honey was dissolved in 10 mL of distilled water and shaken for one hour. An aliquot of 1 mL of this solution was mixed with 1 mL of DNS reagent and incubated in a boiling water bath for 2 minutes. After cooling for 10 minutes, the absorbance was measured at 570 nm using a UV-Vis spectrophotometer (Shimadzu 1601 PC, Japan). A standard calibration curve was prepared using glucose solutions ranging from 2 to 10 mg mL−1. The analysis was performed in triplicate.

sec.title: Color intensity and optical density
sec.p: The color intensity of the honey was determined by diluting Honey samples to 50% (w/v) with Milli-Q water and filtered through a 0.45 µm filter. The absorbance of the filtered solution was measured at 450 nm and 720 nm using a spectrophotometer. The difference in absorbance (A450 – A720) was recorded as the color intensity in mAU.63

sec.title: Determination of pH, free acidity, electrical conductivity, and hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF)
sec.p: The physicochemical properties of the honey samples, including pH, free acidity, electrical conductivity, and hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) content, were determined according to the harmonized methods of the International Honey Commission (IHC) and the Association of Official Analytical Chemists (AOAC). All analyses were performed in triplicate.

For pH and free acidity determination, 10 g of honey was dissolved in 75 mL of freshly prepared carbon dioxide-free distilled water. The pH was measured at room temperature using a calibrated digital pH meter (AD11, Adwa Instruments, Szeged, Hungary) after calibration with standard buffer solutions (pH 4.00 and 7.00; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA). Free acidity was determined by titrating the same solution with standardized 0.05 M sodium hydroxide solution (NaOH; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) to an endpoint of pH 8.30. The results were expressed as milliequivalents per kilogram of honey (meq kg−1).

Electrical conductivity was determined using a digital conductivity meter (AD32, Adwa Instruments, Szeged, Hungary). Honey solutions were prepared by dissolving an amount of honey equivalent to 20 g of dry matter in distilled water and adjusting the final volume to 100 mL. The conductivity meter was calibrated using a 0.01 M potassium chloride (KCl) standard solution (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA), and measurements were performed at 20 ± 0.5 °C. Electrical conductivity was expressed as mS cm−1.

Hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) content was determined by the White spectrophotometric method. Briefly, 5 g of honey was dissolved in distilled water and transferred to a 50 mL volumetric flask. The solution was clarified by sequential addition of Carrez I solution (15% w/v potassium hexacyanoferrate(II) trihydrate; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) and Carrez II solution (30% w/v zinc acetate dihydrate; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA), followed by dilution to volume with distilled water and filtration through Whatman No. 1 filter paper (Cytiva, Marlborough, MA, USA). The absorbance of the filtrate was measured at 284 and 336 nm using a UV–Vis spectrophotometer (UV-1900i, Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan), and the HMF concentration was calculated from the absorbance difference (A284 – A336) according to the White equation. Results were expressed as mg kg−1 honey.

sec.title: Total phenolic content (TPC)
sec.p: The total phenolic content (TPC) of the honey samples was determined using the Folin–Ciocalteu colorimetric assay as previously described, with minor modifications. Briefly, 400 µL of honey solution (1 g dissolved in 10 mL distilled water) was mixed with 3.0 mL of 10% (v/v) Folin–Ciocalteu reagent (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA). After 5 min, 3.0 mL of 7% (w/v) sodium carbonate (Na2CO3; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) was added, and the reaction mixture was incubated at 40 °C for 30 min. Following cooling to room temperature, the absorbance was recorded at 760 nm using a UV–Vis spectrophotometer (UV-1900i, Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan). Gallic acid (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) was used to construct a calibration curve (40–200 µg mL−1), and the TPC was expressed as milligrams of gallic acid equivalents per 100 g of honey (mg GAE 100 g−1). All measurements were performed in triplicate.64

sec.title: Total flavonoid content (TFC)
sec.p: The total flavonoid content (TFC) of the honey samples was determined using the aluminum chloride colorimetric method with minor modifications. Briefly, 100 µL of honey solution (1 g dissolved in 10 mL distilled water) was mixed with 100 µL of 20% (w/v) aluminum chloride (AlCl3; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) and one drop of glacial acetic acid (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA). The reaction volume was adjusted to 5.0 mL with 70% (v/v) ethanol, mixed thoroughly, and incubated at room temperature for 40 min. The absorbance was recorded at 415 nm using a UV–Vis spectrophotometer (UV-1900i, Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan). Quercetin (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) was used as the reference standard to generate a calibration curve (200–1000 µg mL−1), and the TFC was expressed as milligrams of quercetin equivalents per 100 g of honey (mg QE 100 g−1). All measurements were performed in triplicate.65

sec.title: General phytochemical profiling
sec.p: Phytochemical profiling of honey samples was performed using an Agilent 1200 HPLC system coupled to an Applied Biosystems 4000 Q Trap mass spectrometer. Chromatographic separation was achieved on an Agilent Infinity Lab Poroshell 120 EC-C18 column (3.0 mm × 100 mm, 1.9 µm) with a flow rate of 0.5 mL min−1. The mobile phase consisted of 2 mM formic acid in water (Eluent A) and methanol (Eluent B). A linear gradient was applied as follows: 0–3 min, 100% A; 10 min, 75% A; 14 min, 40% A; and 18 min, 100% B. The mass spectrometer was equipped with an electrospray ionization (ESI) source operating in both positive and negative ion modes. The ESI probe voltage was set to +3500 V and −3500 V, respectively, with a fragmentor voltage of 110 V and a source temperature of 325 °C. The nebulizing and drying gas (N2) pressure was 55 psi. Spectra were acquired over a mass range of m/z 40–600.

sec.title: Detection of methylglyoxal (MGO)
sec.p: Sample preparation for MGO analysis was adapted from a Sigma-Aldrich application note for the analysis of α-dicarbonyls in Manuka honey.66 For both fennel and Manuka honey samples, 10 g of honey was dissolved in a water/ethanol mixture (3 : 2, v/v), and the volume was adjusted to 66.7 mL to obtain a final honey concentration of 150 mg mL−1. Subsequently, 133 mg of o-phenylenediamine (OPD; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) was added to achieve a final OPD concentration of 0.2% (w/v). The reaction mixtures were thoroughly mixed and stored at 8 °C for 48 h to allow complete derivatization of methylglyoxal (MGO) to its stable 2-methylquinoxaline derivative. The derivatized samples were then subjected to LC-MS analysis under the chromatographic conditions described above.

sec.title: Assessment of antioxidant activity
sec.p: The free radical scavenging activity of the honey samples was evaluated using the 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) assay, as previously reported.67 Briefly, 500 µL of a 10% (w/v) honey solution was mixed with 2.5 mL of a methanolic DPPH solution (3.9 mg DPPH in 100 mL methanol). The DPPH reagent (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) was freshly prepared immediately before use. The reaction mixture was incubated in the dark at room temperature for 30 min, after which the absorbance was recorded at 517 nm using a UV–Vis spectrophotometer (UV-1900i, Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan). A reagent blank containing methanol in place of the honey solution was prepared under identical conditions.

sec.title: Biological evaluation of manuka and fennel honey
MTT assay on vero cells
sec.p: The cytotoxicity of fennel and Manuka honey was evaluated in Vero (African green monkey kidney epithelial) cells using the MTT assay (3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide) as previously described.66 Vero cells were obtained from the Holding Company for Biological Products and Vaccines (VACSERA, Giza, Egypt) and maintained in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM; Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) supplemented with 10% (v/v) fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and 1% (v/v) penicillin–streptomycin solution (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Cells were cultured at 37 °C in a humidified incubator containing 5% CO2 and subcultured at 70–80% confluence.

Cells were seeded into 96-well plates and allowed to adhere overnight before treatment with fresh culture medium containing fennel or Manuka honey at final concentrations of 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 6.25, 12.5, 25, and 50 mg mL−1. Following 48 h of incubation, the treatment medium was removed and replaced with 100 µL of MTT solution (0.5 mg mL−1 in serum-free DMEM; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA). After incubation for 4 h at 37 °C, the resulting formazan crystals were dissolved in 100 µL of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA), and the absorbance was measured at 570 nm using a microplate reader (ELx800, BioTek Instruments, Winooski, VT, USA). Cell viability was expressed as the percentage of viable cells relative to untreated control cells, which were considered to represent 100% viability. All experiments were performed in triplicate.68

sec.title: SRB assay on HSF cells
sec.p: The cytotoxicity of fennel and Manuka honey toward human skin fibroblast (HSF) cells was evaluated using the sulforhodamine B (SRB) assay as previously described.67 HSF cells were obtained from the Holding Company for Biological Products and Vaccines (VACSERA, Giza, Egypt) and maintained in Roswell Park Memorial Institute medium (RPMI-1640; Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) supplemented with 10% (v/v) fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and 1% (v/v) penicillin–streptomycin solution (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Cells were cultured at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2 and routinely subcultured using trypsin–EDTA upon reaching 70–80% confluence.

Cells were seeded into 96-well plates and allowed to adhere overnight before treatment with fresh culture medium containing fennel or Manuka honey at final concentrations of 0.1, 0.5, and 1.0 mg mL−1. After 48 h of incubation, the cells were fixed by adding 100 µL of cold 10% (w/v) trichloroacetic acid (TCA; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) to each well and incubating at 4 °C for 1 h. The plates were washed five times with distilled water, air-dried, and stained with 100 µL of 0.4% (w/v) sulforhodamine B (SRB; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) prepared in 1% (v/v) acetic acid for 30 min at room temperature. Unbound dye was removed by washing the plates five times with 1% (v/v) acetic acid, followed by air-drying. The protein-bound dye was dissolved in 200 µL of 10 mM Tris base (pH 10.5; Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA), and the absorbance was measured at 515 nm using a microplate reader. Cell viability was expressed as a percentage of the untreated control, and all experiments were performed in triplicate.69

sec.title: Wound healing (scratch) assay
sec.p: The wound-healing potential of fennel and Manuka honey was evaluated using an in vitro scratch assay on human skin fibroblast (HSF) cells. HSF cells were obtained from the Holding Company for Biological Products and Vaccines (VACSERA, Giza, Egypt) and cultured in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM; Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) supplemented with 10% (v/v) heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA), 100 U mL−1 penicillin, and 100 µg mL−1 streptomycin (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Cells were maintained at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2.

For the scratch assay, HSF cells were seeded into collagen-coated 12-well plates at a density of 2 × 105 cells per well and cultured overnight until a confluent monolayer was formed. Uniform linear scratch with an initial width of approximately 0.80 mm was generated using a sterile 200 µL pipette tip. Detached cells were removed by gently washing the wells twice with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS; Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Fresh complete medium containing the indicated concentrations of fennel or Manuka honey was then added, while control wells received complete medium without honey. Cells were incubated under standard culture conditions (37 °C, 5% CO2), and images of the scratch area were acquired at the specified time points using Images were acquired using an inverted microscope (Leica Microsystems, Wetzlar, Germany). The cell-free wound area was quantified by manually tracing the wound boundaries in digital images using Fiji/ImageJ software (National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA).70 The percentage of wound closure was calculated according to the following equation:Wound closure (%) = (A0 − At)/A0 × 100where A0 is the wound area immediately after scratching (0 h) and At is the wound area at the corresponding time point (24 or 48 h). Data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD).

sec.title: Determination of MIC for fennel and honey samples
sec.p: The antibacterial activity of fennel and Manuka honey was evaluated by determining the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) against Escherichia coli ATCC 25922, Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 29213, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa ATCC 27853 using the broth microdilution method according to the Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) guidelines. Bacterial strains were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA). Cation-adjusted Mueller–Hinton broth (CAMHB; Oxoid, Basingstoke, UK) was used as the test medium.

Fresh honey stock solutions were prepared immediately before each experiment by dissolving 10.0 g of honey in CAMHB and adjusting the final volume to 10.0 mL at ≤37 °C to obtain a 100% (w/v) stock solution (1000 mg mL−1). The solutions were sterilized by membrane filtration through a 0.22 µm syringe filter (MilliporeSigma, Burlington, MA, USA) and serially diluted two-fold in CAMHB.

MIC assays were performed in sterile, flat-bottom 96-well microplates in three independent experiments. Honey solutions were prepared at twice the desired final concentration and mixed with an equal volume of bacterial suspension adjusted to 1 × 106 CFU mL−1, resulting in a final inoculum of 5 × 105 CFU mL−1 in each well. Final honey concentrations ranged from 50% to 0.098% (w/v), corresponding to 500–0.98 mg mL−1.

To compensate for the intrinsic colour and turbidity of the honey samples, uninoculated wells containing the corresponding honey concentrations were included as background controls. Growth control wells containing bacteria without honey and sterility control wells containing uninoculated CAMHB were included in each experiment. Gentamicin (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) was used as the positive control for S. aureus and P. aeruginosa, whereas ceftriaxone (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) served as the positive control for E. coli. Following aerobic incubation at 37 °C for 24 h, bacterial growth was assessed by measuring the optical density at 600 nm using a microplate reader (BioTek Instruments, Winooski, VT, USA). Background-corrected absorbance values were obtained by subtracting the absorbance of the corresponding uninoculated honey control from each inoculated well. The MIC was defined as the lowest honey concentration that completely inhibited visible bacterial growth relative to the growth control.

sec.title: Network pharmacology analysis
sec.p: To investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying the wound healing properties of fennel honey, a network pharmacology approach was employed. Potential molecular targets of the identified compounds in fennel honey were predicted using the PharmMapper and SwissTargetPrediction web servers.71 A comprehensive list of genes associated with “wound healing” was retrieved from the GeneCards database. The overlapping targets between the predicted compound targets and the wound healing-related genes were identified using the Venny 2.1.0 tool.

Functional significance of these overlapping targets was elucidated through Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analyses using the INPUT 2.0 server. A protein–protein interaction (PPI) network was constructed from the overlapping targets with a high confidence score threshold of 0.7. Finally, gene distribution analysis was performed to identify key targets significantly correlated with the biological activity.72,73

sec.title: Molecular docking
sec.p: PI3K Following the identification of the PI3K signaling pathway as a principal target by systems pharmacology, we performed molecular docking to investigate the binding interactions of key fennel honey constituents. The crystal structure of PI3Kα (PDB: 3HHM) was prepared, and the 3D structures of the primary bioactive compounds from fennel honey were optimized. Using the CB-Dock2 server, a blind docking protocol was executed to predict the binding affinity and pose of each compound within the enzyme's active and allosteric sites.74 The resulting poses were ranked by their docking scores, and the top-ranked interaction for the most promising ligand was visualized with Discovery Studio Visualizer to analyze its specific binding mode.75

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All experiments were performed in triplicate, and the results are presented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD). Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism version 10.0 (GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA). Differences among groups were analyzed by one-way analysis of variance (one-way ANOVA), followed by Dunnett's post hoc test for multiple comparisons against the untreated control group. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
